pos: n. (Marcus Tullius Cicero, 106–43 B.C., Roman orator, statesman and philosopher, whose testimony to a universal sense of deity Calvin cites at the opening of the Institutes)
etymology: Latin family name, from cicer, chickpea. Called Tully by older English writers. Author of On the Nature of the Gods, On Duties and the lost Hortensius.
biblical_def: Cicero was the master of Latin prose and the great transmitter of Greek philosophy to Rome. For the church he became a witness, not a teacher. Calvin opens his argument on the knowledge of God by quoting ‘the heathen man’ that there is no nation so barbarous, no people so savage, as to lack the conviction that there is a God. That is Paul's own argument: “that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them” (Rom 1:19), so that “they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). Cicero also wrote finely of a true law, right reason agreeing with nature, the same at Rome and at Athens; and Paul grants that the Gentiles “shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness” (Rom 2:15). Augustine owed his first love of wisdom to Cicero's Hortensius, and Lactantius was called the Christian Cicero. Yet the same Cicero who knew there was a God argued on both sides of the question of the gods, and died in the civil wars without the knowledge of the Saviour. He shows what natural revelation can do: it can leave a man without excuse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines orator as a public speaker; one who pronounces a discourse publicly on some special occasion; and, in a more limited sense, an eloquent public speaker.
webster_full: ORATOR, n. A public speaker. In ancient Rome, orators were advocates for clients in the forum and before the senate and people.
2. In a more limited sense, an eloquent public speaker; a speaker by whose arguments an assembly is swayed.
3. In chancery, one who prays for relief; a petitioner.
scriptures: Rom 1:19
Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Rom 2:14
For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves:
Rom 2:15
Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;)
corruption_summary: Cicero is cited by moderns as proof that virtue and natural law need no revelation; Calvin and Paul cite him as proof that men know enough of God to be condemned.
corruption_paragraphs: The natural-law tradition, revived in recent conservative thought, often appeals to Cicero to show that reason alone can establish a public morality common to believers and unbelievers. There is truth in it: the law is written on the heart, and pagan moralists saw parts of it clearly. But Paul's purpose in Romans 1–2 is not to found a common morality; it is to shut every mouth, Gentile as well as Jew, before the judgment of God.

The recovery is to use Cicero as Calvin used him: as an unwilling witness that the knowledge of God is universal, and therefore that the suppression of it is universal sin. Natural revelation leaves men inexcusable; only the gospel saves them.
roots_summary: Greek phaneros (G5318), manifest, evident; anapologetos (G379), without excuse; suneidesis (G4893), conscience.
usage: “that which may be known of God is manifest in them” (Rom 1:19) — Cicero's universal sense of deity.
“so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20) — what that knowledge accomplishes.
“the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom 2:15) — the truth in Cicero's natural law.

pos: n. (Publius Vergilius Maro, 70–19 B.C., Roman poet of the Aeneid, over whose Dido Augustine wept as a boy, and whose lines on a world-soul Calvin rejects in the Institutes)
etymology: Latin Vergilius, a Roman family name; the spelling Virgil arose in the Middle Ages from a fancied link with virgo, maiden.
biblical_def: Virgil was the school author of the Latin world, and every educated boy learned the Aeneid by heart. Augustine confesses that he was made to weep for Dido, who killed herself for love of Aeneas, while he did not weep for himself, dying from God in those very studies. He calls it madness to grieve over a fiction and be dry-eyed over one's own soul. Calvin quotes Virgil's famous lines that a spirit within nourishes heaven and earth and a mind diffused through the frame moves the whole mass, and answers that this world-soul talk puts a shadowy deity in the place of the living God who made all things. Paul, at Athens, did quote a pagan poet: “as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring” (Act 17:28) — but to turn his hearers from images to the Creator. Paul bids the believer think on “whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report” (Php 4:8), and that liberty reaches what is truly lovely in such poetry. The gods it celebrates are another matter: “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines poet as the author of a poem; the inventor or maker of a poetical composition; one skilled in making poetry.
webster_full: POET, n. The author of a poem; the inventor or maker of a poetical composition; one skilled in making poetry, or who has a particular genius for metrical composition.
2. One distinguished for poetic talents.
scriptures: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Ecc 1:2
Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
corruption_summary: Augustine's tears over Dido are the classic diagnosis of a soul that feels deeply about stories and not at all about God, and they describe an entertainment culture more precisely than any modern critic.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader is moved to tears by novels, films and songs, and treats that capacity as a sign of a refined heart. Augustine found it the opposite: proof that his affections were fully alive and wholly misdirected, lavished on the death of an imaginary queen while his own soul perished unmourned. A Christian can weep at a story and pray for nothing; the tears are not the measure of the heart.

The recovery is not to burn the Aeneid. Augustine's later mastery of Latin served the church, and Paul quoted the poets. It is to order the affections, so that the soul is first grieved for sin and moved by the death of Christ, and only then free to enjoy what is lovely in human art.
roots_summary: Greek poietes (G4163), maker, poet; prosphiles (G4375), lovely, pleasing; Hebrew hebel (H1892), vanity, vapour.
roots_lines: Greek poietes (G4163) — a maker, poet, doer; Acts 17:28, James 1:22.
Greek prosphiles (G4375) — lovely, acceptable; Philippians 4:8, the only use.
usage: “as certain also of your own poets have said” (Act 17:28) — how Paul used the pagan poets.
“whatsoever things are lovely” (Php 4:8) — the liberty to enjoy what is good in them.
“Vanity of vanities” (Ecc 1:2) — Augustine's verdict on weeping for Dido.

pos: n. (Plutarch of Chaeronea, c. 46–c. 120, Greek biographer and moralist, priest at Delphi, author of the Parallel Lives, the Moralia and the essay On Superstition)
biblical_def: Plutarch was the most widely read moralist of the ancient world, and his Lives of the Greeks and Romans shaped the idea of character for every educated age down to the American founders. He was also a priest of Apollo at Delphi in the very generation after Paul, and he is a fair witness to what Paul found at Athens: a religious, thoughtful, superstitious world. Plutarch wrote that a traveller might find cities without walls, without letters, without kings, but never a city without temples and gods. Paul's sermon on Mars' hill begins from the same fact: “Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious” (Act 17:22), and he found an altar “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” (Act 17:23). Plutarch's own essay On Superstition condemned the terror of the gods, but his cure was a gentler piety, not the knowledge of the true God. Romans 1 gives the verdict on the whole learned tradition he represents: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22), because “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God” (Rom 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superstition as excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples in the observance of religious rites not commanded.
webster_full: SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples in the observance of religious rites not commanded.
2. False religion; false worship.
3. Belief in the direct agency of superior powers in certain extraordinary or singular events.
scriptures: Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
Rom 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Rom 1:22
Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,
corruption_summary: Plutarch is admired as the moralist who rose above superstition, and he illustrates the error of treating refined religion as nearer to God than crude religion.
corruption_paragraphs: The enlightened reader likes Plutarch because he disdained the vulgar fear of the gods and preferred a reasonable, ethical piety. Modern comparative religion makes the same move, ranking religions by their sophistication and assuming that the philosophical believer is closer to the truth than the superstitious one. Paul makes no such ranking at Athens. Philosophers and idol-worshippers alike were worshipping ignorantly, and both were commanded to repent.

The recovery is the gospel's levelling. The priest of Delphi with his moral essays and the peasant with his amulet stand in the same need, for neither knows the God who made the world. The Lives may still teach much about the shape of virtue and vice, but they cannot give the righteousness of Christ.
roots_summary: Greek deisidaimon (G1174), superstitious, very religious; agnostos (G57), unknown; moraino (G3471), to become foolish.
roots_lines: Greek deisidaimon (G1174) — reverencing demons, very religious; Acts 17:22.
Greek agnostos (G57) — unknown; Acts 17:23, the only use.
Greek moraino (G3471) — to make or become foolish; Romans 1:22, 1 Corinthians 1:20.
usage: “I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious” (Act 17:22) — Plutarch's Greece.
“TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” (Act 17:23) — the altar behind all his piety.
“Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22) — the verdict on the learned tradition.

pos: n. (Xenophon of Athens, c. 430–c. 354 B.C., soldier and historian, pupil of Socrates, author of the Anabasis and the Memorabilia, cited by Calvin on the religion of Socrates)
biblical_def: Xenophon led the retreat of the Ten Thousand Greeks out of Persia and told the story in the Anabasis, the schoolbook of generations of Greek students. He was also a disciple of Socrates, and in the Memorabilia he defended his master's piety. Calvin reports from Xenophon that Socrates praised the answer of Apollo bidding every man worship the gods according to the custom of his own city, and observes that this is the end of even the wisest heathen: when the best of them came to religion, they fell back on custom. Paul faced the heirs of that school at Athens, where “certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him” (Act 17:18). “the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom” (1Co 1:22); but the wisdom they sought could not find God, for “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1Co 1:25). Solomon had laid down the beginning that Socrates lacked: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines custom as frequent or common use or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; habitual practice; established manner.
webster_full: CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; habitual practice.
2. Established manner; usage.
3. In law, long established practice, or usage, which constitutes the unwritten law.
scriptures: For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.

Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
corruption_summary: Xenophon's Socrates, worshipping according to the custom of his city, is the patron of every modern religion that treats inherited practice as sufficient warrant for worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The relativist assumption that each people rightly worships in its own way, and that the outsider should respect the custom of the city, is older than modernity; Calvin found it in Socrates through Xenophon. It reappears today in the multicultural instinct that missions are an imposition and that religion is a heritage to be preserved rather than a truth to be tested.

The Reformed answer is the regulative principle. God is to be worshipped not according to the custom of any city but according to His own appointment in Scripture. Socrates had the honesty to admit his ignorance; the gospel gives what he lacked, the knowledge of the true God in Christ.
roots_lines: Greek philosophos (G5386) — a lover of wisdom; Acts 17:18, the only use.
usage: “the Greeks seek after wisdom” (1Co 1:22) — the school of Socrates and Xenophon.
“the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1Co 1:25) — the answer to it.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7) — the beginning Socrates lacked.

pos: n. (Demosthenes, 384–322 B.C., Athenian orator, whom Calvin sets beside Cicero to show that Scripture moves the heart as no eloquence can)
biblical_def: Demosthenes was the greatest orator of Greece, whose speeches against Philip of Macedon were studied for two thousand years as the summit of persuasive art. Calvin uses him in a famous passage of the Institutes. Read Demosthenes or Cicero, Plato or Aristotle, he says, and they will delight, move and enrapture you; then turn to the sacred volume, and it will so affect you, so pierce your heart, so fix itself in your very marrow, that their force beside it will vanish. That is the Scripture's testimony to itself: “the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12); “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). Paul renounced the orator's art on purpose: “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4), “That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1Co 2:5). The comparison is not between good and bad style; it is between the voice of man and the voice of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oratory as the art of speaking well, or of speaking according to the rules of rhetoric, in order to persuade.
webster_full: ORATORY, n. The art of speaking well, or of speaking according to the rules of rhetoric, in order to persuade.
2. Exercise of eloquence.
3. Among the Roman Catholics, a close apartment near a bed-chamber, furnished with an altar, a crucifix, etc. for private devotions.
scriptures: And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
corruption_summary: Demosthenes stands for the confidence that the right words, rightly delivered, can change men, and the modern pulpit's dependence on communication technique is that confidence baptised.
corruption_paragraphs: Preaching today is often taught as a branch of communication: structure, illustration, delivery, audience analysis, the arts of the orator applied to the Bible. Much of it is useful, and Calvin himself wrote excellent Latin. But when the sermon's power is located in the craft, the preacher has quietly become a Demosthenes, and the faith of his hearers stands in the wisdom of men.

Calvin's comparison is the corrective. The Scriptures, even plainly read, do what no orator can do, because God speaks in them. The preacher's task is to open the Word faithfully and get out of its way; the fire and the hammer belong to God.
roots_summary: Greek apodeixis (G585), demonstration, proof; Hebrew pattiysh (H6360), hammer; Greek energes (G1756), powerful, effective.
roots_lines: Greek apodeixis (G585) — a showing forth, demonstration; 1 Corinthians 2:4, the only use.
usage: “not with enticing words of man's wisdom” (1Co 2:4) — Paul's refusal of Demosthenes' art.
“sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12) — the force no orator has.
“like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces” (Jer 23:29) — the Word Calvin set beside the speeches.

pos: n. (Nero Claudius Caesar, 37–68, Roman emperor from 54, the Caesar to whom Paul appealed and the first emperor to persecute Christians at Rome)
etymology: Latin Nero, a Sabine cognomen said to mean strong, valiant. Not named in the New Testament, which calls him simply Caesar.
biblical_def: Nero was emperor when Paul wrote to the Romans, and that fact gives Romans 13 its edge: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1) was written to Christians living under the man who would burn them. It was to Nero's court that Paul appealed from Festus: “I appeal unto Caesar” (Act 25:11). During his Roman imprisonment the gospel reached the palace itself, for he sends greetings from “they that are of Caesar's household” (Php 4:22). After the great fire of Rome in 64, Nero fastened the blame on the Christians, and the historian Tacitus records that they were torn by dogs, crucified, and burned as torches in his gardens. The church has always held that Peter and Paul died at Rome in his reign. Paul's last letter shows the spirit in which he faced it: “At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me” (2Ti 4:16); “Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me” (2Ti 4:17). Nero died by his own hand in 68, abandoned by the senate and the guard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tyrant as a despot; a monarch or other ruler who uses power to oppress his subjects; a person who exercises unlawful authority, or lawful authority in an unlawful manner.
webster_full: TYRANT, n. A monarch or other ruler or master, who uses power to oppress his subjects.
2. A despotic ruler; a cruel master; an oppressor.
3. Among the ancient Greeks, one who seized the government of a state without right.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar.
Php 4:22
All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household.
Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
corruption_summary: Nero is the test case for Romans 13, and both its modern misreadings — that Christians owe any government unlimited obedience, and that a wicked government forfeits all obedience — break against him.
corruption_paragraphs: One misreading treats Romans 13 as a charter for whatever the state commands; but Paul, who wrote it, disobeyed Rome's ban on preaching Christ and died for it. The opposite misreading treats any unjust ruler as no ruler at all; but Paul wrote of Nero's government as ordained of God and appealed to its courts. Paul held both: the office is God's, and the ruler answers to God for how he bears it.

The recovery is the apostolic pattern: honour the office, use the courts, pray for rulers, obey in all things lawful, refuse what God forbids, and suffer what must be suffered. The Christians in Nero's gardens did not revolt, and they did not deny Christ. Their blood, not their politics, conquered Rome.
roots_summary: Greek exousia (G1849), power, authority; epikaleo (G1941), to appeal to, call upon; endunamoo (G1743), to strengthen.
roots_lines: Greek epikaleo (G1941) — to call upon, appeal to; Acts 25:11, 12.
Greek endunamoo (G1743) — to empower, strengthen; 2 Timothy 4:17, Philippians 4:13.
usage: “there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1) — written to Christians under Nero.
“I appeal unto Caesar” (Act 25:11) — Paul's use of Nero's courts.
“chiefly they that are of Caesar's household” (Php 4:22) — the gospel inside Nero's palace.

pos: n. (Dioscorus of Alexandria, d. 454, patriarch from 444, who presided over the violent ‘Robber Synod’ of Ephesus in 449 and was deposed at Chalcedon in 451)
etymology: Greek Dioskouros, ‘son of Zeus,’ after the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux.
biblical_def: Dioscorus succeeded Cyril as patriarch of Alexandria and pressed Cyril's party far beyond Cyril. When Eutyches was condemned at Constantinople for confusing the two natures of Christ, Dioscorus took up his cause. At the council he presided over at Ephesus in 449, with imperial soldiers and a crowd of monks at his back, he restored Eutyches, refused to allow the letter of Leo of Rome to be read, and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who was so roughly handled that he died soon after. Leo called the gathering not a council but a robbery, and the name stuck. Paul had foreseen such men: “of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30), as Paul also warned, “after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock” (Act 20:29). A bishop is to be “patient, not a brawler” (1Ti 3:3). At Chalcedon in 451 Dioscorus was deposed, and the council confessed one Christ in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. He died in exile, and the churches that refused Chalcedon still honour him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines violence as physical force; force applied to the injury of persons or things; outrage; unjust force.
webster_full: VIOLENCE, n. Physical force; strength of action or motion.
2. Moral force; vehemence.
3. Outrage; unjust force; force employed against rights, laws or liberty.
scriptures: For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
corruption_summary: Dioscorus shows that an orthodox-sounding party can carry a heresy by force, and that the church's councils are to be judged by Scripture and not by who controls the room.
corruption_paragraphs: Dioscorus claimed to defend the faith of Cyril against the Nestorians, and his council had every outward mark of legitimacy: a summons from the emperor, bishops in session, a formal decree. It is a standing warning against judging councils by their procedure or their claims. The Reformed confess that councils may err and many have erred, and that their decrees are to be received only so far as they agree with the Word of God.

The opposite modern error treats every doctrinal council as a power play, as though Chalcedon were no better than Ephesus II. Leo and Flavian were right, and the Chalcedonian definition faithfully guards what Scripture teaches of Christ. The recovery is to test both by the Word, and to see that truth can be outvoted for a season without ceasing to be truth.
roots_summary: Greek lukos (G3074), wolf; diastrepho (G1294), to pervert, twist; plektes (G4131), striker, brawler.
roots_lines: Greek plektes (G4131) — a striker, pugnacious man; 1 Timothy 3:3, Titus 1:7.
usage: “speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30) — the Robber Synod.
“patient, not a brawler” (1Ti 3:3) — the bishop Dioscorus was not.
“I withstood him to the face” (Gal 2:11) — why Flavian and Leo were right to resist.

pos: n. (Epiphanius of Salamis, c. 315–403, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, author of the Panarion against eighty heresies, who tore down a painted image of Christ or a saint from a church curtain)
biblical_def: Epiphanius was a learned and combative bishop who spent his life cataloguing heresies. His Panarion, or ‘medicine chest,’ describes eighty of them with antidotes, and preserves much that would otherwise be lost. He is remembered by Protestants for a letter to John of Jerusalem, which Jerome translated: passing through the village of Anablatha, he went into a church and found a curtain over the door painted with the image of Christ or of some saint. He tore it down, saying it was against the authority of Scripture to hang a man's image in the church of Christ, and gave money for a plain curtain in its place. That is the second commandment applied: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4), and Moses' reason for it: “ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb” (Deu 4:15), “Lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image” (Deu 4:16). He spent himself contending “for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), though with more zeal than judgment in his quarrels over Origen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines image as a representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; an idol.
webster_full: IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; as an image wrought out of stone, wood or wax.
2. A statue.
3. An idol; the representation of any person or thing that is an object of worship.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Deu 4:15
Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:
Deu 4:16
Lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image, the similitude of any figure, the likeness of male or female,
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Epiphanius's torn curtain refutes the claim that the veneration of images was the faith of the ancient church; a fourth-century bishop thought an image of Christ in a church a breach of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The Second Council of Nicaea (787) and Rome and Orthodoxy after it present the veneration of images as apostolic tradition, and accuse those who reject it of a later iconoclasm. Epiphanius's letter, from the end of the fourth century, shows a revered bishop, famous for his zeal against heresy, treating a painted image in a church as contrary to the Scriptures. The tradition the image-venerators claim was not unanimous; the earlier witness is against them.

The recovery is the second commandment as the Reformed Confessions read it: God is to be worshipped only in the way He has appointed, and He has forbidden every likeness made for worship. Evangelicals who decorate their sanctuaries with images of Jesus have drifted further than they know from both Epiphanius and Moses.
roots_summary: Hebrew pesel (H6459), graven image; temunah (H8544), similitude, form; Greek epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesel (H6459) — an idol, carved image; Exodus 20:4, Deuteronomy 4:16.
usage: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the law Epiphanius applied to a curtain.
“ye saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15) — why no image of God may be made.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jud 1:3) — the labour of the Panarion.

pos: n. (Zephyrinus, d. 217, bishop of Rome c. 199–217, whom his contemporary Hippolytus accused of tolerating the modalist teaching that the Father Himself suffered)
etymology: Latin from Greek Zephurinos, from zephuros, the west wind.
biblical_def: Zephyrinus led the Roman church at the turn of the third century, during the controversy over the teaching of Noetus and Sabellius that Father, Son and Spirit are one Person appearing in three modes, so that the Father became incarnate and suffered. His presbyter Hippolytus, a learned opponent of the modalists, wrote that Zephyrinus was an ignorant man, open to bribes, led by his deacon Callistus, and that he publicly made statements that favoured the heresy. Whatever the exact truth of the charges, they show that the early Roman bishops were not regarded by their own clergy as infallible guardians of doctrine. The faith that answered modalism was the faith of the baptismal command, three Persons and one name: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19). The Word who became flesh “was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1); the Son prays to the Father to send “another Comforter” (Joh 14:16). The apostolic benediction distinguishes and unites them: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost” (2Co 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines person as an individual human being; and, in theology, as applied to the Trinity, a distinct subsistence in the one divine essence.
webster_full: PERSON, n. An individual human being consisting of body and soul.
2. A human being represented in dialogue or on the stage; a character.
3. In theology, the unknown manner of subsistence by which the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are distinguished in the one Godhead.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
corruption_summary: Zephyrinus's reported toleration of modalism undercuts Rome's claim to an unfailing papal orthodoxy, and modalism itself is the most common Trinitarian error in evangelical pews today.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome teaches that the faith of the bishop of Rome has never failed. A Roman presbyter of the time said that Zephyrinus and his successor Callistus favoured the error that confused the Persons of the Godhead. The Reformed do not rest the doctrine of the Trinity on any bishop; they rest it on Scripture, which is why it can survive a weak or compromised pope.

Modalism has a modern popular form in the illustration of one man who is a father, a son and a husband, or of water as ice, liquid and steam. Such pictures teach Sabellius, not the creeds. The recovery is to confess with the 1689 Confession one God in three distinct Persons, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, of one substance, power and eternity.
roots_summary: Greek onoma (G3686), name; parakletos (G3875), Comforter, advocate; koinonia (G2842), communion, fellowship.
roots_lines: Greek onoma (G3686) — name, singular over three Persons; Matthew 28:19.
Greek parakletos (G3875) — one called alongside, Comforter; John 14:16, 26, 1 John 2:1.
usage: “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19) — against every modalism.
“the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — distinct and one.
“another Comforter” (Joh 14:16) — the Spirit is not the Son under another name.

pos: n. (Eulogius of Alexandria, d. 607/608, patriarch from c. 580, to whom Gregory the Great wrote refusing the title of ‘universal pope’)
biblical_def: Eulogius was patriarch of Alexandria, a defender of Chalcedon against the monophysites and a friend and correspondent of Gregory the Great. When Eulogius, writing to Gregory, addressed him as ‘universal pope,’ Gregory refused the title. He asked Eulogius not to use it, saying that what is given to another beyond what reason demands is taken from oneself, that he did not count it an honour by which his brethren lost their honour, and that words which inflate vanity and wound charity should be put away. He had already called the same title, when the patriarch of Constantinople claimed it, proud and profane. Calvin quotes these letters in the Institutes against the later papacy, which claims exactly what Gregory refused. Gregory's refusal stands under Christ's command: “be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). “he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger” (Luk 22:26). “whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased” (Mat 23:12). “be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud” (1Pe 5:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines title as an appellation of dignity, distinction or pre-eminence given to persons; as, the title of duke, lord or bishop.
webster_full: TITLE, n. An inscription put over any thing as a name by which it is known.
2. An appellation of dignity, distinction or pre-eminence given to persons.
3. A claim; a right.
scriptures: Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.
But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
corruption_summary: The letter to Eulogius is Rome's own pope condemning Rome's later claim, and it shows that the universal primacy of the bishop of Rome was not the faith even of its most honoured bishop.
corruption_paragraphs: The papacy now teaches that the bishop of Rome holds full, supreme and universal power over the whole church. Gregory the Great, a Doctor of the Church in Rome's own reckoning, refused the title of universal pope from Eulogius and denounced it as pride when another bishop claimed it. The development from Gregory's refusal to the decrees of the First Vatican Council is not the unfolding of a seed; it is the reversal of a principle.

The recovery is Gregory's own better instinct, grounded in Christ's words: in Christ's church there is one Master and all others are brethren. Pastors receive honour as servants and stewards, and every title that lifts one man above his brethren in the house of God is to be put away.
roots_lines: Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — lowliness of mind, humility; 1 Peter 5:5, Philippians 2:3.
usage: “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8) — why Gregory refused the title.
“he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger” (Luk 22:26) — the rule for every bishop.
“God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble” (1Pe 5:5) — the end of all universal titles.
